title: p-Adic statistical field theory of fluctuation effects in hierarchical neural networks
abstract: The Buice-Cowan field theory [PRE 75, 051919 (2007)] describes fluctuations and correlations of neural activity through a path integral whose mean-field limit is the Wilson-Cowan equation and whose critical behavior belongs to the directed percolation class. In its continuum limit the neurons are the points of a Euclidean space and activity spreads by ordinary diffusion, which encodes neither the hierarchical organization of cortical networks nor their small-world property. We formulate a version of the theory in which the neurons are organized in an infinite, self-similar, tree-like structure, described by the p-adic numbers. The path integral carries over unchanged, and finite networks are exact restrictions of the continuum theory. The main change is in the linear response: in the Euclidean theory every short-range kernel reduces to the Laplacian, while in the p-adic theory each connectivity kernel gives its own nonlocal p-adic diffusion operator. For couplings that decay by a fixed factor per level of the hierarchy this is the Taibleson-Vladimirov operator, and the critical theory is an ultrametric Reggeon field theory whose upper critical dimension is twice the decay exponent of the coupling. Hence the decay of the coupling up the hierarchy, and not the dimension of space, decides whether mean-field exponents apply. We obtain a Ginzburg-type criterion, loop-corrected hierarchical Wilson-Cowan equations, log-periodic corrections to scaling and power-law correlations. Exact simulations on a tree support the predictions: the avalanche-size exponent takes the mean-field value 3/2 when the coupling decays slowly and decreases toward the directed-percolation value when it decays fast. The hierarchical network is also small-world when the decay exponent is smaller than the dimension, a property that the Euclidean theory obtains only by assuming long-range coupling.
summary: This paper develops a p-adic statistical field theory to model fluctuations in hierarchical neural networks, addressing shortcomings of classical Euclidean models. By mapping the network structure onto p-adic numbers, the authors derive a nonlocal diffusion operator and predict critical exponents and small-world behavior governed by the coupling decay rate. This provides a mathematically rigorous framework for understanding complex, structured systems beyond standard continuum approximations.
main_problem: To formulate a statistical field theory describing fluctuation effects in hierarchical neural networks, overcoming the limitations of standard Euclidean models regarding network structure and small-world properties.
main_result: The theory successfully models the network using p-adic numbers, yielding an ultrametric Reggeon field theory whose critical behavior depends on the coupling decay exponent rather than the embedding dimension.
method: The authors adapt the path integral formulation to the p-adic space, replacing the standard Laplacian with a nonlocal p-adic diffusion operator, and performing detailed loop calculations (one-loop and two-loop self-energies).
model_or_system: The model is a neural network organized in an infinite, self-similar, tree-like structure described by p-adic numbers. It is compared against the standard Buice-Cowan theory which uses Euclidean space.
key_observables: Avalanche-size exponent, small-world property, power-law correlations, and the two-loop self-energy ($\Sigma_A, \Sigma_B$).
important_parameters: The coupling decay exponent ($\sigma$), the dimension ($N$), and the critical exponents derived from the Ginzburg criterion.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the p-adic structure providing exact restrictions of the continuum theory, and the calculations involve assuming absolute convergence for the complex p-adic integrals.
figures_summary: Not specified in the notes, but the comparison between Euclidean and p-adic theories is central.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the p-adic framework and comparing it to the Euclidean B-C theory, then deriving the necessary mathematical tools (lemmas for p-adic integration), and finally applying these tools to calculate higher-order correlation functions (one-loop and two-loop self-energies).
why_interesting: The mathematical machinery developed for p-adic field theory and its application to complex, structured systems like neural networks provides novel tools for analyzing non-local correlations and critical phenomena in complex many-body systems, which has parallels in quantum many-body physics.
